$comment: Rule-panel spec for anti-slop-adoption-arc inc-05 — the BATCHED panel. Four target rules against the two controls inc-04 proved, in ONE packet: the builder takes N specimens, the controls amortise across all four targets, and the blinding gets stronger with more rules, not weaker (panel-procedure.md §5a). Build with: storytree lint-panel packet --spec <this> --report <oxlint.json> --out-dir <dir>
codebaseContext:
The sites below are drawn from one TypeScript monorepo: roughly two dozen libraries under
`packages/*` and three applications under `apps/*`, on Node with pnpm workspaces. What matters
for judging the rules:

- **Compiler settings.** `strict` is on, and so are `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`,
  `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, and `verbatimModuleSyntax`. Module resolution is `NodeNext`, so
  relative imports carry a `.js` extension. There is no build step — packages export raw
  TypeScript, consumed through `tsx`.
- **A document-store seam.** `packages/storage-protocol` declares a narrow document/event store
  contract that several backends implement (in-memory, Postgres, and an HTTP front door). It is a
  DOCUMENT store: it persists and returns documents without knowing their shapes. Readers on the
  far side validate what they receive with zod schemas before using it.
- **A schema-first domain tier.** `packages/library` and `packages/proof-protocol` declare zod
  schemas for the domain objects — work-hierarchy nodes, knowledge documents, signed verdicts.
  The intended discipline is that validation happens at boundaries and validated objects flow
  inward.
- **A large command surface.** `packages/cli` is a single CLI with many verbs, most of which front
  another package's competence. `packages/drive` holds shared build/orchestration drivers.
- **Two UI applications.** `apps/studio` is a React app with a Node backend serving a JSON API;
  `apps/desktop` is an Electron app whose backend mirrors a subset of the studio's routes.
- **Foreign-data readers.** Several packages exist specifically to read data this project does not
  own and cannot change: a coding agent's newline-delimited JSON session transcripts, a foreign
  CLI's event stream on stdout, third-party `settings.json` files, and the JSON output of external
  tools. These packages parse and correlate that material; the schemas are the vendors', are
  undocumented, and change without notice.
- **Procedural geometry and rendering.** `packages/forest-world-r3f`, `packages/app-surface` and
  `packages/procedural-architecture` generate 3D and 2D scenes programmatically — meshes built
  from vertices and facets, terrain, tree canopies, building parts — and render them through
  three.js and SVG. Geometric modelling vocabulary is the working vocabulary of these packages.
- **Testing.** `node:test` with `node:assert/strict`. Test files sit beside their sources as
  `*.test.ts` and are not shown below.

The codebase has no linter of any kind today. These rules are candidates for its first one, and
would be enforced as errors in continuous integration if adopted.

specimens.statement: A runtime `typeof` check must not be used to decide how a value is handled. `typeof` reports how a value is REPRESENTED — string, number, object, function — and a representation is not a contract. Knowing a value is a string tells you nothing about whether it is an identifier, a path, a serialised timestamp or an error message; knowing it is an object tells you nothing about which object. Branching on the representation therefore commits the program on the weakest evidence available, at the point furthest from where that evidence could have been strengthened, and it leaves no record of what the value was supposed to be — so the next reader cannot tell a deliberate contract from a defensive guess. Decode input into a named domain type at the boundary where it enters the program, with a schema, a parser or a constructor, and branch on the domain value afterwards. Once that boundary exists, every representation check downstream is either redundant or is compensating for a boundary that was never established.

No symbol name may contain the word "shape", in any casing, anywhere in the identifier. Naming a thing for its structure rather than for its role in the domain is the commonest way a program loses the meaning it was written with: it says that a value has fields, which is true of very nearly every value, and says nothing about what the value IS, who owns it, what produced it, or what a reader may do with it. Worse, a structural name survives every refactor unchanged while the thing it names drifts underneath it, so it stops carrying information and becomes decoration that reads like documentation. Every symbol named this way has a real domain role available to it — the thing it classifies, the decision it feeds, the boundary it crosses, the owner it belongs to — and the remedy is to name it for that instead. The rule is deliberately absolute: a term this weak has no position in which it is the best available name.

A function parameter must not be annotated `unknown`. A parameter list is a contract with every caller, and `unknown` states that contract as `anything at all` — which does not remove the obligation to establish what the value is, it relocates it inward, to a body that knows LESS about the value's provenance than the caller did. The caller knew where the value came from; the function now has to rediscover it, and will do so with whatever ad-hoc checks are to hand. Accept a named domain type, and run the schema or parser that produces that type at the I/O boundary where the value actually enters the program, so the check happens once, in the place that has the information to do it, instead of being repeated by every function downstream. The single exception the rule keeps is an error `cause`, where the value genuinely originates outside any contract this program controls.

A function's declared return type must not be `unknown`, nor `Promise<unknown>`, nor an alias or union that resolves to one. A return type is the strongest promise a function makes, and this one makes none: every caller must independently re-establish what came back, each of them with less information than the function that produced it, and any two callers that disagree will do so silently. The producing function is the one place in the program where the value's provenance is actually known — it performed the read, the call, or the decode — so it is the one place the type can be established honestly rather than assumed. Parse the value where it is produced and return the named domain type; a function that cannot say what it returns has not finished doing its job, it has deferred it.

A type assertion must not be routed through an intermediate widening — the shape written `x as unknown as T`, where the direct `x as T` would be rejected. The chain exists precisely to silence a rejection: the compiler declined the conversion because it could not see the two types as sufficiently related, and passing through a top type supplies none of the missing relationship — it only removes the question. Assert once, so the compiler still has to find the narrowing plausible, and change the types when it does not.
specimens.expected:
UPHOLD. Held independently of this panel by the compiler, before any panel sat: this codebase reduced all of its production chains to single assertions, and THREE were then rejected outright as false — a hand-written module mirror missing seven fields of the real type it claimed to be, a declared dictionary value type the document provably violated (`schemaVersion` is a number), and a `window` shape that contradicted the ambient global declaration of the same object. That is ground truth from a checker, not an opinion, so a panel that REJECTS this rule has failed a control with a known answer.

CALIBRATION FROM inc-04, where this same control ran on the same panel shape: it returned `adopt-narrowed` x5, never `adopt` x5 and never a reject. Every judge independently drew the same line — permit the chain where the assertion target CLAIMS NOTHING (an index-signature or all-`unknown` bag) and error where it asserts a concrete contract. So `adopt-narrowed` x5 here is the instrument REPEATING, and is a PASS; a plain `adopt` sweep would be a (benign) drift and a `reject` anywhere is a FAIL.

specimens.statement: Type-only bindings must not be imported through a statement separate from the value bindings they accompany. A module's dependency on another module is one fact, and splitting it across `import type { A } from './m'` and `import { b } from './m'` states that fact twice: a reader scanning the head of a file sees two entries for one relationship, and any tool that walks import statements has to reconcile them. Import every binding a module needs from a given module through a single `import { ... }` statement.
specimens.expected:
REJECT. This is a SYNTHETIC rule authored for inc-04's panel — no upstream tool implements it, and it is in the packet only to test whether the panel can refuse a plausibly-worded rule rather than agree with everything put in front of it. It should be rejected on FUNCTIONALITY grounds, which is the hardest available: the codebase context states that `verbatimModuleSyntax` is on, and under that setting a type-only binding imported through a value import is emitted as a runtime import of something that does not exist at runtime. Complying would break the build.

CALIBRATION FROM inc-04: rejected 5-0 at high confidence, with every judge reaching `verbatimModuleSyntax` unaided and several noting the rule's own duplication rationale does not apply to most of the evidence at all. A judge who UPHOLDS this has not read the codebase context against the rule; a judge who rejects it on style alone has read it less carefully than one who names the compiler setting. Anything other than a reject sweep is a FAIL.
